771.title: Egeria's diary
771.hook: a woman traveled to the Holy Land and wrote down how Jerusalem kept Holy Week
771.howItsDone: Christians make pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela and other holy places, and some churches walk in procession with palms on Palm Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nicholas: gold through a window by night, and a plea to tell no one. Your line: a gift by night.

Dear sisters. That's who she's writing to: a circle of women back home, somewhere in the west, who can't make the trip. So she makes it for them, and writes it all down. Her name, as it reaches us, is Egeria. She travels through the lands of the Bible, climbs mountains, asks the local monks and clergy to show her where the stories happened, and reads the passage aloud on the spot. Then, in Jerusalem, she writes down, day by day, how the church there keeps Holy Week, the days before Easter. Because of her notebook, we can stand in that crowd.

Palm Sunday first. The people gather with their bishop on the Mount of Olives, then walk down into the city together, carrying branches of palm or olive. Children too small to walk ride on their parents' shoulders. All the way down they sing the line the crowds sang for Jesus: "Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord." They aren't just remembering the story; they're walking it, on the same hill. That's pilgrimage: a journey to a holy place, where the walking itself becomes a prayer. Now Good Friday, and a startling detail. The bishop sits with the wood of the cross on a table before him, held in his hands, deacons standing around. The people come forward one by one, bow, touch it with their forehead and eyes, and kiss it. The deacons guard it closely, she explains, because once someone bit off a piece and ran off with it. Holiness and human nature, side by side. The bishop preaches in Greek, but not everyone understands Greek, so a priest beside him translates into Syriac, and others explain it for those who speak Latin. A crowd from everywhere, in one city, each hearing it in their own words. A psalm about going up to Jerusalem begins, "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD." Egeria went, and wrote it down so her sisters could walk where she walked, without leaving home.

Then find one small detail you'd almost forgotten, the kind Egeria wrote down, and hold it as if for someone who couldn't be there.
Pilgrimage. A journey to a holy place, where the walking itself becomes a kind of prayer, and where, for Egeria, the story was read aloud on the very spot.
Your line: walk where they walked. Some journeys are made for the ones at home. Day seven hundred seventy-one, done.

772.title: Pachomius' community
772.hook: monks living together under a rule: work, prayer, shared bread
772.howItsDone: Christian monks and nuns in Orthodox, Catholic and other traditions live in community under a rule, sharing work, prayer at set hours, and meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Egeria's diary and pilgrimage, the walking that becomes a prayer. Your line: walk where they walked.

Locked up with other recruits in a city on the Nile, rounded up for the emperor's army, sits a young man who isn't a Christian. He's hungry and far from home. In the evening, strangers come with food and drink for the prisoners. He asks who they are. Christians, he's told: people who are kind to strangers, for the sake of the God of heaven. His name is Pachomius. His Life says that night he promised that, if he got free, he would spend his life serving others. A few days ago, Antony walked out alone into the desert. Pachomius goes too, but he doesn't stay alone.

After his release, Pachomius is baptized and learns the hard life of a hermit from an old monk. Then, at a deserted village by the river called Tabennesi, the story goes, he's told to build a place where many could live together. So he does, and it gets hard. His first followers, the Life says, took advantage of him. He served them, cooked, did the chores, and they treated him like the help. He gave them a rule, and when they wouldn't keep it, he sent them away. Living together was harder than living alone. So Pachomius organized it. Monks lived in houses, each with a leader. They worked with their hands, weaving mats and baskets, and the work supported the community and the poor. They prayed at set times and ate together, the same food at a shared table. The sick were cared for. Nobody owned anything privately. People kept coming, and more communities were founded along the river. Acts had already described this way of life among the first Christians in Jerusalem: "they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." The Greek word behind fellowship there is koinonia, a life held in common, and Pachomius' communities came to be called by that name: the Koinonia. Alone in a cave, nobody leaves dishes in your sink. Nobody snores. Nobody needs you when you're tired. In community, everyone does. As the Life tells it, for Pachomius that was the point.

Bring to mind the people you share space or work with, and notice the small friction points, the dishes, the trash, the one always late, without stewing. Then pick one chore that usually falls to one person and imagine doing it alongside them, not instead of them, the way Pachomius' monks shared the work and the bread. If you pray, pray for the people you live with, by name.
Pachomius' community. The shared life Pachomius built by the Nile: houses of monks under a rule, with work, prayer and bread held in common.
Your line: together is harder, and better. The dishes are part of it. Until next time.

773.title: Basil's new city
773.hook: Basil of Caesarea built a place of care for the poor and sick, and his friend called it a new city
773.howItsDone: Churches and Christian orders run hospitals, clinics, hospices, shelters and food banks, and church members give to and volunteer in them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pachomius' community: monks sharing work, prayer and one table. Your line: together is harder, and better.

"I will pull down my barns, and build greater." That's the rich man in one of Jesus' parables, in Luke's Gospel. His harvest is huge, so he plans bigger storage, and that night his life is asked of him. Basil, then a priest in Caesarea, in what's now central Turkey, and later its bishop, preached on that line to his own people. In his time, a famine came to his city, and the rich, like the man in the parable, had full barns. Basil had a sermon, a pulpit, and a gift for making people uncomfortable. By the end he's built, on the edge of town, what his close friend would call a new city.

The famine first. His friend Gregory tells it, in a speech in Basil's memory. Basil opened the storehouses of those who had them, by the force of his preaching. He gathered the hungry in one place and served them himself, with his own hands, alongside his helpers. In his sermon on the barns, Basil pushes hard. In paraphrase: the bread you keep in store belongs to the hungry; the coat in your closet belongs to the one without one. He isn't asking for leftovers. He's asking whose the extra really is. Then he builds. Outside Caesarea, Basil put up a whole complex: lodging for travelers and strangers, a place for the poor, care for the sick, with people to nurse them and workers to keep it going. A local governor was apparently uneasy. Basil wrote to him: what harm does this do the state? We're housing strangers and caring for the sick. Go a little way out of the city, Gregory says in paraphrase, and look at the new city, a storehouse of devotion, where the rich put their surplus. And he singles out the people others avoided: those with the disease that disfigured skin and drove sufferers out of town. Basil didn't keep his distance. He greeted them, embraced them, even kissed them, as brothers. Not a building, but a bishop bending down to kiss someone everyone else had sent away.
screen: `THE FAMINE: HE SERVED WITH HIS HANDS.`

774.title: Gregory of Nazianzus
774.hook: a shy poet-bishop who preached on the Trinity in a tiny church and resigned rather than fight
774.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians honor Gregory as a teacher of the faith, calling him the Theologian, and Catholic and other churches keep his feast; his sermons on God are still read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Basil, who built a new city of care outside Caesarea. Your line: a city of mercy.

Two students in Athens who know only two roads: one to church, one to their teachers. That's how Gregory remembers himself and Basil, in his speech in Basil's memory. Gregory, from a small town called Nazianzus, is today's word. He loved books, quiet and poetry. What he didn't love was being in charge. When his own father, a bishop, made him a priest, Gregory ran away to think it over, and later wrote a long defense of why he'd fled. And yet this reluctant man was about to be sent into the middle of a fierce religious argument in the empire's new capital.

The capital was Constantinople, and the argument was the one we met at Nicaea, still raging. There, the people holding to the Nicene creed were few, and had lost their churches. So Gregory preached in a small house chapel, given by a relative, and named it Anastasia: resurrection. A small room, standing for a faith he hoped would rise again. There he preached a series of sermons on God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. They're careful and humble. He keeps saying that talking about God is dangerous, that God is beyond our words, and that the way to know God is a clean, prayerful life, not winning debates. Later tradition gave him a title: Gregory the Theologian. Then the tide turned. A new emperor favored the Nicene side, the great churches were handed back, and Gregory, the shy poet, was put in charge of the city's church. At the council held there, he presided for a time. And then the fights began, about him. Rival bishops said his appointment broke the rules. Factions formed. By his own account, Gregory reached for the prophet Jonah, who told the sailors in the storm: "Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you." He resigned. He went home to Cappadocia, wrote poems, including a long one about his own life, and cared for a small flock. He didn't keep the job. He chose the calm over the chair.

Think of a fight you're in, or about to be in, that doesn't really need to happen, where being right has started to matter more than anything you're defending, and picture it as a boat in a storm. Ask what would actually be lost if you stepped back: sometimes something real, and then you stay; sometimes only your position. If you pray, bring that fight to God and leave it there for now.
Gregory. Basil's friend from Nazianzus, a poet and preacher on the Trinity, who led the church in Constantinople and stepped down rather than keep a fight going.
Your line: peace over position. A poet's choice, and not an easy one. See you tomorrow.

775.title: Macrina
775.hook: the older sister who taught her brothers Basil and Gregory, and led a community at home
775.howItsDone: Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor Macrina as a saint, and Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Macrina and his dialogue with her are read as spiritual classics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregory of Nazianzus, who chose the calm over the bishop's chair. Your line: peace over position.

In a whole book of conversation with his older sister, a bishop hardly ever calls her by her name. He calls her the Teacher. He's Gregory of Nyssa, Basil's younger brother, also a bishop and a deep writer; not yesterday's Gregory, Basil's friend from Nazianzus. His sister was Macrina. She never became a bishop. She didn't preach at councils. And yet her brother wrote her life, as well as that book.

Gregory's Life of Macrina starts at the beginning. She was the eldest child. As a girl, she was engaged to a young man who died before the wedding. Her family wanted to arrange another match. She refused. In her view, Gregory says, she was still promised to him, a man alive to God, and she would wait for the resurrection. So she stayed home with her mother and the younger children. Then Basil came home from his studies, and Gregory is startlingly frank about his famous brother. In paraphrase: Basil came back excessively proud of his skill as a speaker, looking down on everyone important in town. Macrina took him in hand, drawing him toward a simpler life, away from fame, toward God. The Basil we met two days ago, kissing the sick outside his new city, had a sister behind him. Then Macrina turned her household into a community. She persuaded her mother to live on equal terms with the women who had been their servants: the same table, the same work, the same prayers. Rank dissolved around the dinner table. She also raised and taught her youngest brother, Peter, who became a bishop too. At the end of her life, Gregory came to see her, heavy with grief after Basil's death. She was dying, and she comforted him, and the two talked about the soul and the resurrection. He wrote it down as a dialogue, with her as the Teacher, and himself as the student who keeps asking questions. A woman at home, teaching brothers who would go on to teach the church.

Bring to mind someone who was a Macrina for you: an older sister, a cousin, an aunt, a coach, a coworker who showed you the ropes, someone who taught you without a title and maybe took you down a peg when you needed it. Remember one specific thing they did or said, and hold it. If you pray, thank God for them, by name.
Macrina. The older sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, who drew her brothers toward God and led a community at home, and whom Gregory called the Teacher.
Your line: the teacher of teachers. No title needed, and no pulpit either. Day seven hundred seventy-five, done.

776.title: Constantinople (381)
776.hook: the council completes the creed: the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life
776.carry: the lord, the giver of life
776.howItsDone: Christians in Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches say the Nicene Creed together in worship, Orthodox churches without the words and the Son, most Western churches with them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Macrina, the older sister her brother called the Teacher. Your line: the teacher of teachers.

The creed from Nicaea spent a long time on the Son. Begotten, not made. Of one substance with the Father. Then it reached the Holy Spirit and said, in effect, just this: and in the Holy Spirit. Full stop. For a while that seemed enough. Then people began asking the same kind of question about the Spirit that Arius had asked about the Son. Is the Spirit God, or a power God sends, or something God made? So bishops gathered again, in Constantinople, the city that carried Constantine's name, where Gregory had preached in his small chapel and then stepped down. What they added is still said in churches.
screen: `NICAEA: AND IN THE HOLY SPIRIT. FULL STOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the fuller creed that came out of Constantinople, in the old English of the Book of Common Prayer. On the Spirit, it now says: "And I believe in the Holy Ghost, The Lord and giver of life." Two titles. First, Lord: the same word the creed uses for Jesus, a title that belongs to God. Second, giver of life. In the Greek that's one word, zoopoion, the life-maker. Some readers hear in it Genesis, where God forms the first human from the dust and "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." And Jesus in John's Gospel: "It is the spirit that quickeneth." Quickeneth: makes alive. The next line is where churches today differ. The council's Greek says the Spirit proceeds from the Father. Later, in the West, the words and the Son were added, and the Prayer Book text has them. Orthodox Christians say the creed without those words. In the West, Catholic Christians, and Protestant churches that use the creed, generally say it with them. That phrase has been argued over for a long time. Then the creed adds: "Who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified, Who spake by the Prophets." Worshipped together: not a lesser helper, but one God, Father, Son and Spirit. This is the creed later called, simply, the Nicene Creed. So the creed said in churches on Sunday carries both councils, and its closing section, on the Spirit, runs on to the church, baptism and the life to come.
screen: `THE LORD: A TITLE THAT BELONGS TO GOD.`
`THE GIVER OF LIFE: BREATH IN THE DUST.`

segments.voice: Let your breathing slow, and notice the breath coming in without forcing it. Genesis pictures life starting with a breath, so let each breath in be the words giver of, and each breath out, life; if you pray, you can say the creed's line silently instead: the Lord, and giver of life. If you don't, simply notice the breath arriving on its own.
Constantinople. Constantine's city, where bishops met again and completed the creed's words on the Holy Spirit: the Lord, the giver of life.
Your line: the lord, the giver of life. Two councils, one creed, still said on Sundays. Rest well.

777.title: Ambrose and the emperor
777.hook: after a massacre, Bishop Ambrose makes Emperor Theodosius do public penance
777.howItsDone: Christians remember Ambrose as a saint and a bishop of Milan; the story of Theodosius' penance is retold as an example of repentance and of a pastor's courage before power.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantinople, and the Spirit. Your line was the lord, the giver of life.

A city has just been punished by its own emperor. In Thessalonica, after a riot, Emperor Theodosius orders a reprisal, and soldiers kill the people gathered in the city's circus. The old historians say the guilty and the innocent died together. The emperor is a baptized Christian. His bishop in Milan, Ambrose, has known him well. Now Ambrose has to decide what a bishop does when a man with that much power has blood on his hands.

Two kinds of evidence tell it differently. The first is a letter from Ambrose himself, careful, almost tender. He wrote it in his own hand, he says, so the emperor alone would read it. He cannot offer the sacrifice of the altar with the emperor present, not until he repents. And he reminds him of King David. David also sinned terribly, and the prophet Nathan told him a story about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb. David burned with anger at the rich man, until Nathan said, in the King James words, "Thou art the man." David confessed. A king who repents, Ambrose says, is not made smaller by it. The second account is a scene, from the historian Theodoret. The emperor arrives at the church in Milan, and Ambrose meets him at the door and won't let him in. Theodosius says that David sinned too. Ambrose answers: you followed him in sinning, now follow him in repenting. Readers handle Theodoret's drama with care; the letter is quieter. But the sources agree on what came next. The emperor did public penance before the people, and only then was received back to communion. At his funeral, Ambrose recalled it: Theodosius took off the signs of his royalty and wept for his sin in church. Days ago on this path, an emperor's favor turned the church from hunted to favored. Here is the edge of that favor. Ambrose was no rebel, but he would not pretend. He wrote alone first, and left a door open. Some see the church standing over the throne; others, a conscience standing before a ruler. Both start from Nathan's line.
screen: `A PRIVATE LETTER, IN HIS OWN HAND.`

segments.voice: Let one person with power over others come to mind, someone whose choice troubles you. If anger comes, set it beside you, and ask what Ambrose seems to have asked: what would a true word sound like, said privately, with a door left open? Just find the sentence, and if you pray, hold that person before God by name.

Ambrose. The bishop who said no to an emperor, first in a letter, until the ruler set aside the signs of his royalty to repent. That ends a week of a pilgrim, monks, a city of mercy, a poet, a teacher, and a creed.
Your line: no one is above it. Not even an emperor on his throne. See you tomorrow.

myth: Ambrose's first word to the emperor was a public rebuke
his own letter was private, written in his own hand for the emperor alone.
Theodosius set aside the signs of his royalty to repent
Ambrose said so at the emperor's funeral: he wept for his sin in church.
Ambrose's letter and Theodoret tell the story the same way
Theodoret tells a dramatic scene at the church door; Ambrose's letter is quieter. they agree on the penance.

fork.setup: you're Ambrose. the emperor, a friend of the church, has ordered a massacre. what do you do?
options: say nothing: he protects the church.
write to him privately, and hold back communion until he repents.
denounce him to the crowd before you say a word to him.
fork.reveal: Ambrose wrote alone first, reminding him of David. the penance became public, but the first word was private, and it left a door open.

original.note: Greek: repentance, a change of mind. the New Testament word for turning around.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bishop scolded an emperor.
what it means: after a massacre, a bishop held back communion until a baptized emperor repented, and the emperor did, in public.
what a scholar hears: two kinds of evidence. Ambrose's private letter, invoking Nathan and David, and Theodoret's later, more dramatic scene at the church door.
recall: the old bishop who served Christ 86 years
the sister her brothers called the Teacher
guess: a bishop of Milan who called an emperor to repent

a historian who wrote the scene at the church door

chat.says: Did a bishop really stand up to an emperor? How did he go about it?
options: First a private letter in his own hand, asking him to repent, with a door left open.
He led a public revolt in Milan and had the emperor removed from his throne.
He let it pass, since an emperor's choices weren't really a bishop's business.
chat.meaning: Ambrose wrote alone first, in his own hand, and kept the emperor from communion until he repented. Then Theodosius did public penance.

Thessalonica.meaning: a Greek city where the emperor's soldiers killed a crowd

Nathan.meaning: the prophet who told King David: thou art the man

Theodoret.meaning: an ancient church historian who tells the scene at the door
